# Free Mandarin Learner's Dictionary
  License: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International)
  Based on the English-Chinese Wiktionary: https://en.wiktionary.org/
  Wiktionary data imported from https://kaikki.org (January 2025)
  All entries with a "w" tag contain data from Wiktionary and should be attributed accordingly.
  
  Words up until "%" are sorted roughly by frequency. After "%" the entries are initially sorted by codepoint,
  new entries can be inserted anywhere so it's not strictly ordered.
  
  
  Format Description
  
  - encoded in utf-8
   - character variant mapping: 裏->裡
  - single indentation (space or tab) creates a child element
  - double indentation relative to previous line continues previous line (intended for notes and comments)
  - the first letter indicates the content of the line:
    * W: word and optional variants
    * P: pronunciation in pinyin with tone marks, 5 for neutral tone
         allowed characters: A-Z; a-z; 1-5; v for ü; additionally: ê. -,
    * C: class / part-of-speech
    * D: definition
    * X: cross-reference, the X is followed by another character indicating the type of reference
         (symmetric) means that the reference should exist in both directions
      * =: synonym-equal (symmetric)
      * ~: synonym-similar (symmetric)
      * !: antonym (symmetric)
      * ?: could-be-confused-with (symmetric)
      * %: cross-strait (symmetric) (mnemonic: the line in % is the Taiwan strait)
      * <: part-of
      * >: contains
      * V: word-variant-of
      * v: character-variant-of
      * M: used-with-measure-word
      * L: collocation
      * G: word-group (e.g. North, South, East, West)
    * #: comment (meta information etc. which is not relevant to readers of the dictionary)
    * N: note, e.g. more detailed explanations
      * N->: direct reference to a note entry to avoid duplications in the text representation
  - allowed child elements for each entry type:
    * W: P, X, #, N
    * P: P (one level, to attach notes to individual pinyins), C, #, N
    * C: D
    * D: D (definitions can be nested), X, #, N
    * X: #, N
    * #: none
    * N: none
  - every entry must have at least one definition, leading to he following minimum structure: W->P->C->D
  - notes and definitions can contain references to words using brackets like [嗎／吗]
    or [嗎／吗#D1] if the link is to a single definition
  
  
  Grammar (EBNF)
  
  {} is repeated zero or more times (like *)
  [] is repeated zero or one time (optional)
  
  entry_line = "W" tags_ascii word_entry {; word_entry}
  pinyin_line = "P" tags_ascii pinyin {; pinyin} {tags_ascii pinyin {; pinyin}}
  class_line = "C" ascii_word
  definition_line = "D" id [tags_full] ...
  cross_reference_line = "X" ascii_symbol tags_ascii reference {; reference} {tags_ascii reference {; reference}}
  comment_line = "#" ...
  note_line = "N" ("?" | id) ...
  note_reference_line "N->" id ...
  
  id = ? 1-9 {0-9}
  ascii_symbol = any non-special, visible ASCII character excluding |
  tag_letter = A-Za-z0-9 and "-"
  tag_word = tag_letter {tag_letter}
  hanzi = anything except "|#;/／"
  hanzi_word = hanzi {hanzi}
  pinyin_letter = A-Za-z0-9 and "ê. -,"
  pinyin = pinyin_letter {pinyin_letter}
  word_entry = hanzi_word [("／" | "/") hanzi_word]
  reference = word_entry [#D id]
  tags_ascii = "|" {ascii_symbol} "|"
  tags_full = "|" {ascii_symbol} {"#" tag_word} "|"
  
  
  Editing 
  
  New notes should be added with a note id ? or a number <100. They will be automatically replaced with a new id.
  The current maximum note id is linked in the line below:

   D3||Things like straw sandals and hemp sandals were written as '𧆓' in ancient times, which is now simplified to '麤'.
   D9||Alternative form of 粗 (cū, “coarse; rough; rude”)
    D4||robust、Sturdy.如：「麤厲」
    D5||overbearing、brutish.如：「麤豪」
    D6||careless，imprecise.
    D7||rough、coarse.如：「麤茶」
    D8||sketchy、plain.如：「麤具」

 P||di4zhi1
  C noun
   D9||An earthly branch: one of the twelve terms used in East Asian cultures to represent
    D1||(historical astronomy) The (approximately) twelve years of Jupiter's orbital period, forming the Chinese zodiac and personified as twelve or sixty gods known as Tai Sui.
    D2||(astrology) The twelve animals representing the Chinese zodiac, particularly as a birthyear.
    D3||(obsolete) The twelve months of the Chinese lunar year.
    D4||(historical navigation) The twelve bearings of traditional Chinese navigation, comprising 30° divisions of the compass beginning with due north.
    D5||(historical astronomy) The duodecimal divisions of the Chinese seasons, beginning with the second of the three divisions of winter.
    D6||(historical chronometry) The duodecimal divisions of the day into "Chinese" or "double hours", beginning with 11 pm.
    D7||(historical chronometry) The exact time at the middle of a "Chinese" or "double hour", beginning with midnight.
   D8||The twelve earthly branches as a whole.
